clinicalPearls: Dental trauma ranges from enamel fractures through crown-root fractures to luxation and complete avulsion, and injuries frequently coexist
The maxillary central incisors are the teeth most commonly injured, especially in children and young adults
Avulsion of a permanent tooth is a time-critical emergency, as the survival of the periodontal ligament falls rapidly the longer the tooth is out of the socket and dry
An avulsed permanent tooth should ideally be reimplanted promptly or stored in a suitable physiological medium such as milk or saliva rather than water
Avulsed primary teeth are generally not reimplanted because of the risk of damaging the developing permanent successor
Pulp status can change over time after luxation injuries, so baseline and repeated sensibility testing and follow-up are essential
Ellis-type crown fractures involving dentine or pulp need timely protection or pulp management to preserve vitality
Always assess for associated alveolar, jaw, and soft-tissue injuries, and consider non-accidental injury when the history is inconsistent
reference.pathophysiology: Dental trauma results from a direct or indirect force exceeding the resistance of the tooth and its supporting structures. Depending on the vector and magnitude, energy is dissipated as enamel or dentine fracture, pulp exposure, displacement of the tooth within or out of its socket (luxation or avulsion), or fracture of the alveolar bone. Injury to the neurovascular supply at the apex can lead to reversible or irreversible pulpal damage and later necrosis, while disruption of the periodontal ligament and its cells governs the likelihood of successful healing after repositioning or reimplantation. Extra-oral drying and delay compromise ligament cell viability and predispose to replacement resorption.
additionalDifferentials: Pre-existing caries or fracture unrelated to the acute event
additionalInvestigations: Systematic clinical examination of teeth, occlusion, and soft tissues
Pulp sensibility testing at baseline and on follow-up
Periapical and occlusal radiographs, with further imaging for suspected jaw fractures
Assessment of tooth mobility, displacement, and percussion note
Documentation of injury time and storage medium for avulsed teeth
redFlags: Airway compromise, significant haemorrhage, or associated head and facial injuries requiring emergency management
Signs of jaw fracture such as malocclusion, trismus, or step deformity
Inconsistent history or injury pattern suggesting non-accidental injury
Aspirated or unaccounted-for tooth fragments needing chest imaging
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on injury type, maturity of the tooth, and speed of appropriate care; minor fractures and promptly managed luxations often do well, whereas avulsions with prolonged dry time and mature apices frequently develop pulp necrosis or root resorption.
pitfalls: Storing an avulsed tooth in water or letting it dry, damaging periodontal ligament cells
Reimplanting avulsed primary teeth and harming the permanent successor
Assuming an initially vital tooth will remain so and skipping follow-up sensibility testing
Focusing on the obvious dental injury and missing alveolar or jaw fractures or non-accidental injury
management: Treat avulsion of a permanent tooth as a time-critical emergency: reimplant promptly or store in a physiological medium such as milk or saliva, then reimplant and apply a flexible splint
Reposition and splint luxated or displaced teeth and reduce and stabilise associated alveolar fractures
Restore fractured crowns with adhesive composite and manage pulp exposure with pulp capping or pulpotomy, preserving vitality in immature teeth
Do not reimplant avulsed primary teeth because of the risk to the developing permanent successor
Provide endodontic treatment for teeth that develop pulp necrosis and monitor for root resorption
Give tetanus prophylaxis, analgesia and antibiotics where wounds are contaminated
Perform baseline and serial pulp sensibility testing with radiographic follow-up, and plan prosthetic or orthodontic rehabilitation for lost teeth
